question: What minimum RBC ratio does one of LLANY's reinsurance arrangements require, and how does that compare with the RBC range that triggers the regulator's company action level?

answer.text:
One of LLANY's reinsurance arrangements requires LLANY to maintain an RBC ratio of at least 185% (or an S&P capital adequacy ratio of 115%) [5]. LLANY's largest indemnity reinsurance arrangement has a lower minimum of 160% (or an S&P capital adequacy ratio of 100%) [5].

The company action level is triggered when the RBC ratio is between 75% and 100%, which requires the insurer to submit a corrective action plan to the regulator [3][4]. The 185% contractual minimum is therefore 85 percentage points above the top of the trigger range (100%) and 110 points above the bottom (75%). The 160% minimum is 60 points above the top of the range [5][3].

These contractual thresholds are well above the regulatory trigger. If LLANY's RBC ratio fell below them, the cedent could recapture the business under the largest arrangement [5]. For the other arrangements, the excerpt states only the 185% requirement and does not describe the consequence of a shortfall [5]. As of December 31, 2025, the consolidated RBC ratio for LNC's statutory insurance companies was in excess of four times the company action level RBC [4]. This consolidated figure is not specific to LLANY.

question: Why does Principal Financial Group's capacity to return capital hinge on Principal Life, and how much could Principal Life pay out in 2026 without asking the Iowa regulator?

answer.text:
Why it hinges on Principal Life: Principal Financial Group (PFG) is an insurance holding company whose assets include all the outstanding common stock of Principal Life and other subsidiaries. Its ability to pay dividends, repurchase shares, and meet obligations (operating expenses, debt service) depends on receiving dividends or other distributions from Principal Life [2]. Iowa insurance laws limit what Principal Life can send up to its parent, so any inability of Principal Life to pay could leave PFG unable to pay stockholder dividends or meet other obligations [2].

The Iowa rules: Principal Life may pay dividends only from earned surplus arising from its business. It needs prior approval from the Iowa Commissioner of Insurance if a distribution would exceed statutory limits, and the Commissioner has discretion to disapprove requests above those limits [1][3]. Extraordinary dividends are those that, together with other distributions in the preceding twelve months, exceed the greater of (i) 10% of statutory policyholder surplus at the prior year-end (excluding admitted disallowed interest maintenance reserve) or (ii) the prior calendar year's statutory net gain from operations, not to exceed earned surplus [1][3].

The 2026 amount: Based on 2025 statutory results, Principal Life could pay approximately $1,234.0 million in ordinary stockholder dividends in 2026 without prior regulatory approval [3][1].

A caveat: because the test looks at dividends paid over rolling twelve-month periods, some or all dividends paid before a specified date in 2026 may be extraordinary and require approval [5].

For context, Principal Life paid $1,055.0 million to its parent in 2025 and $1,010.0 million in 2024, all of it extraordinary and approved by the Commissioner [5]. PFG also had $2,362.3 million of cash and liquid assets in its holding companies and other subsidiaries at December 31, 2025, available for corporate purposes [5].
